title: Automated Exfiltration
summary: Automated exfiltration is the use of scripted or scheduled processing to move collected data out of a network without a human driving each transfer. Collection still happens first; automation then handles packaging, compression, optional encryption, transfer, and in many cases the deletion of the local copy. Because it runs unattended, it can work slowly over long periods, follow business hours, retry after failures and resume after a reboot, which keeps each individual event small and unremarkable. The pattern usually appears in a host's task scheduler, a cron style job, a service, or a long lived script, while the actual movement rides on a second technique such as the existing command and control channel or an alternative protocol. Detection leans on repetition and process lineage: the same command line running on a timer, archive tools producing files that are uploaded immediately, and outbound transfers whose size and rhythm match no approved job. Telling it apart from legitimate data movement requires a maintained inventory of the approved jobs and their destinations.

beginner.definition: Automated exfiltration means using a script or a scheduled job to send stolen data out of the network. No person has to press a button each time. The job can run at night, in small amounts, or whenever a connection is free. It keeps working even when something fails once.
beginner.whyItMatters: Slow, regular transfers are easy to miss in a busy network. A program that repeats every hour looks like ordinary housekeeping. If nobody checks which jobs are approved, a large theft can run for weeks unnoticed. Automation also means the attacker can disconnect and still collect the data.
howItWorks: The attacker gathers the files they want and stores them in one place.
They compress and sometimes encrypt the data into one or more archives.
They create a script, service or scheduled job that will do the sending.
The job sends the data out on a timer, in small amounts, using another channel.
It retries after failures and may remove local copies once a transfer succeeds.
It keeps running quietly, so the attacker does not need to stay connected.
beginner.example: Imagine a post office clerk who is told to send just one parcel every night at two in the morning. Nobody watches that window, and one parcel never looks strange. Over a year, the whole storeroom leaves in small, tidy boxes. Automated exfiltration is that standing order. The crime is not one dramatic scene. It is a quiet routine that nobody ever thought to question.
takeaways: Small size plus steady repetition is the signature, so compare transfers against approved jobs.
Look for scheduled tasks and services that archive data and then upload it.
Keep a list of your legitimate automated transfers so a new one stands out.

objectives: Define automated exfiltration and explain how it differs from manual transfer.
Describe the stages an automated job performs after the collection step.
Explain why regular, small transfers are difficult to detect on a busy network.
Identify host artefacts such as scheduled tasks, services and script files.
Compare observed outbound transfers with an inventory of approved jobs.
